evidence.claim: An old highway alternate through eroded buttes and mixed-grass prairie
evidence.quote: sharply eroded buttes and pinnacles, along with the largest undisturbed mixed grass prairie in the United States.

evidence.claim: An old highway alternate
evidence.quote: the Badlands Loop was signed as U.S. Route 16 Alternate (US 16 Alt.)

evidence.claim: South Dakota Highway 240, signed as the Badlands Loop, crosses the eastern portion of Badlands National Park.
evidence.quote: South Dakota Highway 240 (SD 240), also signed as the Badlands Loop, is a 40.033-mile-long (64.427 km) state highway in southeastern Pennington and northwestern Jackson counties in South Dakota, United States, that travels through the eastern portion of Badlands National Park.

evidence.claim: The park protects sharply eroded buttes and pinnacles alongside mixed-grass prairie.
evidence.quote: sharply eroded buttes and pinnacles, along with the largest undisturbed mixed grass prairie in the United States.

evidence.claim: Exposed rock records a change from inland sea to river floodplains; erosion continues to shape the badlands.
evidence.quote: The exposed rock records the change from an ancient inland sea to river floodplains.

evidence.claim: A highway was part of the park’s beginnings: the 1929 law authorizing Badlands National Monument made construction of a 30-mile road through it a condition of its eventual proclamation.
evidence.quote: The legislation's conditions for eventual proclamation included the acquisition of privately owned land within the proposed boundaries of the monument and the construction of a 30-mile highway through the park.

evidence.claim: Construction on the highway began in the early 1930s, and the loop had a gravel surface by 1944.
evidence.quote: Construction began in the early 1930s. By 1944, a gravel surface was on the Badlands Loop alignment

evidence.claim: By the late 1940s, it carried the US 16 Alternate number.
evidence.quote: by the late 1940s, the Badlands Loop was signed as U.S. Route 16 Alternate (US 16 Alt.)

evidence.claim: When US 16 was cut back to Rapid City around 1980, its alternate no longer met the parent route and became SD 240.
evidence.quote: Around 1980, US 16, which traveled concurrently with I-90, was truncated at its eastern end to Rapid City. Since US 16 Alt. no longer met the parent route, the route number was changed to SD 240.

evidence.claim: From Wall at Interstate 90’s exit 110, the road runs south into the park and turns southeast.
evidence.quote: SD 240 begins in Wall at exit 110 of Interstate 90 (I-90). It travels south to Badlands National Park, where it turns southeast.

evidence.claim: At park headquarters at Cedar Pass, it turns northeast to rejoin I-90 at exit 131 near Cactus Flat.
evidence.quote: At the Badlands Headquarters at Cedar Pass, the highway turns northeast, ending at exit 131 of I-90 near Cactus Flat.

evidence.claim: erosion continues to shape the badlands.
evidence.quote: The badlands are geologically young and still actively eroding.

evidence.claim: the 1929 law authorizing Badlands National Monument
evidence.quote: On March 4, 1929, his final day in office, President Calvin Coolidge signed Public Law No. 1021.  This bill authorized creation of the Badlands National Monument in South Dakota.

evidence.claim: The park’s exposed rock records the shift from an inland sea to river floodplains.
evidence.quote: The exposed rock records the change from an ancient inland sea to river floodplains.

evidence.claim: Wall began as a railroad town, platted in 1907 when the Chicago and North Western reached this point.
evidence.quote: Wall was platted in 1907 when the Chicago and North Western Railroad was extended to that point.

evidence.claim: Its name comes from the natural wall of rock formations by the Badlands.
evidence.quote: Wall was named for the "natural wall" in rock formations by the Badlands National Park.

evidence.claim: A different kind of traffic helped make it known later: Ted Hustead bought Wall Drug in 1931, and Dorothy Hustead proposed advertising free ice water to travelers heading toward Mount Rushmore.
evidence.quote: Business was very slow until his wife, Dorothy, thought of advertising free ice water to thirsty travelers heading to the newly opened Mount Rushmore monument

evidence.claim: The small pharmacy grew into a roadside attraction.
evidence.quote: The store eventually developed into a large roadside tourist attraction.

evidence.claim: Wall also houses the National Grasslands Visitor Center, a companion subject to the park’s rock formations.
evidence.quote: The National Grasslands Visitor Center is also located in Wall.

evidence.claim: Ted Hustead bought Wall Drug in 1931
evidence.quote: The small-town drugstore made its first step towards fame when it was purchased by Ted Hustead in 1931.

evidence.claim: A national park entrance fee is charged where the highway enters the park.
evidence.quote: Because the highway enters a national park, there is an entrance fee charged along the highway at either entrance to the park.

evidence.claim: Interior moved to meet the railroad.
evidence.quote: In 1907 and 1908, the town was moved two miles and half northwest along the White River to meet the Milwaukee Railroad.

evidence.claim: Its earlier life began as a freighting way-station established by George and Louis Johnson on the White River in 1883.
evidence.quote: Norwegian immigrants George and Louis Johnson moved from Chamberlain, South Dakota to the banks of the White River just north of the Pine Ridge Reservation in 1883 to establish a way-station for freighting between Chamberlain and the Black Hills.

evidence.claim: In 1907 and 1908, the settlement shifted two and a half miles northwest along the river to the Milwaukee Railroad; the previous site became old Interior.
evidence.quote: In 1907 and 1908, the town was moved two miles and half northwest along the White River to meet the Milwaukee Railroad. The former location of the town became known as "old Interior".

evidence.claim: A water system followed in 1910 and an electric grid in 1912.
evidence.quote: in 1910, an efficient water system transporting water directly from the White River to Interior was installed and an electric grid was installed in 1912.

evidence.claim: Interior lies along the White River approximately one mile from Badlands National Park.
evidence.quote: Interior is located along the White River approximately one mile from Badlands National Park.

evidence.claim: The Ben Reifel Visitor Center dates from 1957–58, when it was built under the Mission 66 plan for Badlands National Monument.
evidence.quote: Under the Mission 66 plan, the Ben Reifel Visitor Center was constructed for the monument in 1957–58.

evidence.claim: The monument became a national park in 1978.
evidence.quote: The monument was renamed "Badlands National Park" in 1978.

evidence.claim: The center offers museum exhibits, special programs and a bookstore.
evidence.quote: The Ben Reifel Visitor Center within the park offers a bookstore, special programs, and museum exhibits.

evidence.claim: Nearby, the park’s established trails include Cliff Shelf Nature Trail.
evidence.quote: Badlands National Park has established hiking trails, including Cliff Shelf Nature Trail (located near Ben Reifel Visitor Center)

evidence.claim: The landscape outside has a much longer record: the exposed rocks document an inland sea giving way to river floodplains, and erosion has cut the rocks into walls, buttes and pinnacles.
evidence.quote: erosion has since cut them into the buttes, walls, and pinnacles that give the park its name. The exposed rock records the change from an ancient inland sea to river floodplains.

evidence.claim: The Yellow Mounds expose an old soil that weathered on marine rocks. Above that soil, the White River Group records river and floodplain deposits; volcanic ash from eruptions in the present-day Great Basin survives in the upper beds.
evidence.quote: A deeply weathered soil that formed on the older marine rocks, now exposed as the colorful Yellow Mounds, lies between the two.

evidence.claim: the White River Group records river and floodplain deposits
evidence.quote: The badlands are eroded from the White River Group, a sequence of river and floodplain sediments

evidence.claim: volcanic ash from eruptions in the present-day Great Basin survives in the upper beds.
evidence.quote: Ash from repeated volcanic eruptions in the present-day Great Basin is preserved through the upper beds.

evidence.claim: The original pharmacy stood on Route 16A, the highway number once carried by the loop.
evidence.quote: which opened as a small pharmacy in 1931 during the Depression, located at that time on Route 16A.

evidence.claim: the highway number once carried by the loop.
evidence.quote: the Badlands Loop was signed as U.S. Route 16 Alternate (US 16 Alt.)

evidence.claim: In 1919, 1921 and 1922, roundups brought tourists by train from as far away as Minneapolis.
evidence.quote: In 1919, 21 and 22, the town hosted roundups that tourists traveled by train as far from Minneapolis to see.

evidence.claim: The monument was established to preserve natural scenery and educational resources, with scientific excavation specifically authorized.
evidence.quote: The Badlands National Monument was established in order to preserve the natural scenery and educational resources within its boundaries. The bill authorized specific scientific and educational institutions to excavate within the monument
